title: Jeremiah 28:1–17
context: In that same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, speaks to Jeremiah in the LORD’s house, in the presence of the priests and all the people. Hananiah says the LORD has broken the yoke of the king of Babylon, and that within two full years the vessels of the LORD’s house, Jeconiah, and all the captives will be brought back. Jeremiah answers, first with “Amen!” a wish that the LORD would do so, and then with a word about earlier prophets who spoke of war and pestilence, and about the prophet of peace who is known to have been sent when the word happens. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference as a shared test of that kind, without inventing a new contrast. Hananiah then takes the bar from Jeremiah’s neck and breaks it, and says the LORD will break Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke from all the nations within two full years. Jeremiah goes his way. After that, the LORD’s word comes: Hananiah has broken bars of wood and made bars of iron; the LORD has put a yoke of iron on the nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah tells Hananiah that the LORD has not sent him, and that he has made the people trust in a lie; this year he will die, because he has spoken rebellion. Hananiah dies the same year in the seventh month. The yoke remains the plain sign of serving Babylon. “That same year,” “the beginning of the reign” and “the fourth year” stand together in the heading and should be left as the text states them, without a reconstructed calendar or manuscript claims. Gibeon, Jeconiah, and the dating of the captives may be hedged. 2 Kings 24–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 may be named without harmonizing.

verses.text: That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, spoke to me in the LORD’s house, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, spoke to me in the LORD’s house, in the presence of the priests and of all the people, saying,” The scene is public, in the LORD’s house. Hananiah is named with his father and as a prophet from Gibeon; the site and family should be hedged where the verse does not explain them. “That same year,” “the beginning of the reign” and “the fourth year” stand together here and are not to be forced into one reconstructed scheme, and no manuscript claim is made.

Arminian readers take the heading as Jeremiah’s report of a public confrontation, a real speech before priests and people, not a private dispute hidden from the city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive the date and the names as the book’s setting: Hananiah of Gibeon speaking in the temple in Zedekiah’s fourth year, in the fifth month, in the presence of all the people.

Shared ground: the meeting is public and dated. The relation of “beginning” to “fourth year,” and of “That same year” to chapter 27, may be left unharmonized.

verses.text: “The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hananiah says, “I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.” Hananiah claims the LORD’s own name and title for a word that the yoke is already broken. The yoke, as in the last chapter, is the plain rule of the king of Babylon.

Arminian readers hear a public claim that can be tested. The name of the LORD of Armies does not by itself make the word true; the following verses will set that test.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted formula as Hananiah’s claim to speak for the God of Israel. The content is the breaking of Babylon’s yoke, which the book will place under the LORD’s later verdict.

Shared ground: Hananiah speaks as if the yoke were already broken. The verse records his word, not yet the LORD’s answer to it.

verses.text: Within two full years I will bring again into this place all the vessels of the LORD’s house that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Within two full years I will bring again into this place all the vessels of the LORD’s house that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon took away from this place and carried to Babylon.” The promise is timed: two full years, and the temple vessels home. That is the “now shortly” hope of 27:16, given a number.

Arminian readers hear a specific, testable claim. Two full years is not a vague comfort; it is a deadline the hearers can remember, and it stands against Jeremiah’s longer word about the vessels.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take “two full years” as the heart of Hananiah’s vessel promise, a short return of what Nebuchadnezzar had already taken.

Shared ground: the timetable is short and clear. It will be measured by what happens, as Jeremiah will say.

verses.text: I will bring again to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, with all the captives of Judah, who went to Babylon,’ says the LORD; ‘for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Hananiah also says the LORD will “bring again to this place Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, with all the captives of Judah, who went to Babylon,” “for I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.” The short hope now includes the king and all the captives, not only the vessels. Jeconiah’s identity and the date of that carrying-away may be hedged and compared, without blending, with 2 Kings 24.

Arminian readers hear a complete reversal promised within the same two years: vessels, king, and captives. The people in the temple are being offered a near end to the exile.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same promise as Hananiah’s word in the LORD’s name: Jeconiah and the captives will come home, because the yoke will be broken.

Shared ground: the claim is large and near. Jeremiah has not said this, and the book will test it.

verses.text: Then the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests, and in the presence of all the people who stood in the LORD’s house,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests, and in the presence of all the people who stood in the LORD’s house,” The answer is as public as the claim. Both men are called prophets in this verse; the title here is the book’s description of the two speakers in the temple, not yet the later verdict on who was sent.

Arminian readers take the public setting as important: Jeremiah does not settle the matter in private. Priests and people hear both the promise and the reply.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a temple confrontation, prophet to prophet, before the whole assembly in the LORD’s house.

Shared ground: the reply begins in the same public place. The verse is a scene heading for what Jeremiah will say.

verses.text: even the prophet Jeremiah said, “Amen! May the LORD do so. May the LORD perform your words which you have prophesied, to bring again the vessels of the LORD’s house, and all those who are captives, from Babylon to this place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah said, “Amen! May the LORD do so. May the LORD perform your words which you have prophesied, to bring again the vessels of the LORD’s house, and all those who are captives, from Babylon to this place.” The first word is “Amen!” a wish that the LORD would do what Hananiah has said. Jeremiah does not sneer at the hope of return; he would welcome the vessels and the captives home if the LORD performed that word.

Arminian readers take the Amen as sincere. Jeremiah can wish that such peace would come, and still go on to test whether the LORD has actually spoken it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a real Amen, a prayer that the LORD would perform those words, before the caution that follows. The desire for return is not treated as a fault.

Shared ground: Jeremiah’s first sentence is a wish that it might be so. The test has not yet been spoken.

verses.text: Nevertheless listen now to this word that I speak in your ears, and in the ears of all the people:
verses.arminianNotes:
“Nevertheless listen now to this word that I speak in your ears, and in the ears of all the people:” The “Nevertheless” turns from the wish to a word the whole crowd must hear. Jeremiah claims a hearing in the same public ears that heard Hananiah.

Arminian readers take the call to listen as a real appeal to the assembly. They are not left with only an Amen; they are asked to hear the further word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same turn: a word now spoken in the ears of Hananiah and of all the people, which will set a measure for the promise of peace.

Shared ground: the people are witnesses. The next lines are for them as well as for Hananiah.

verses.text: The prophets who have been before me and before you of old prophesied against many countries, and against great kingdoms, of war, of evil, and of pestilence.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The prophets who have been before me and before you of old prophesied against many countries, and against great kingdoms, of war, of evil, and of pestilence.” Jeremiah places both of them in a longer line. The older prophets often spoke of war, evil, and pestilence, not of a quick peace.

Arminian readers hear a caution from history: a word of disaster has many predecessors, and that fact should make a sudden peace-promise more, not less, careful to test.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same recollection as Jeremiah’s appeal to the older prophetic pattern: war, evil, and pestilence against countries and kingdoms.

Shared ground: the past prophets are named as a standard of comparison. The verse is not yet the test of a peace prophet, but it prepares it.

verses.text: As for the prophet who prophesies of peace, when the word of the prophet happens, then the prophet will be known, that the LORD has truly sent him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“As for the prophet who prophesies of peace, when the word of the prophet happens, then the prophet will be known, that the LORD has truly sent him.” The peace-prophet is known when the word happens. That is a shared, practical test, and Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named here by reference as a related measure, without inventing a new contrast on that passage.

Arminian readers take the happening of the word as the public proof, a test the hearers can in time apply to Hananiah’s two years as well as to Jeremiah’s longer word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the test as Jeremiah states it: the prophet of peace is known to have been sent when the word happens. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may be named by reference as shared ground, not as a new party fork.

Shared ground: fulfillment makes the sending known. The verse does not ask the traditions to divide over the test itself.

verses.text: Then Hananiah the prophet took the bar from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and broke it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Hananiah the prophet took the bar from off the prophet Jeremiah’s neck, and broke it.” The sign is answered with a sign. Hananiah does not wait for the two years; he breaks the bar Jeremiah has been wearing. The yoke remains a plain wooden bar, now broken in public.

Arminian readers take the act as a public counter-sign, meant to persuade the same crowd that the yoke is already as good as broken, a persuasive act the people can be moved by and must still test.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the breaking of the bar as Hananiah’s enacted word, set against the wooden yoke Jeremiah has worn.

Shared ground: the bar is broken in the temple scene. The LORD has not yet interpreted the act.

verses.text: Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, “The LORD says: ‘Even so I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from off the neck of all the nations within two full years.’ ” Then the prophet Jeremiah went his way.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hananiah spoke in the presence of all the people, saying, “The LORD says: ‘Even so I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from off the neck of all the nations within two full years.’ ” Then Jeremiah went his way. The broken bar is given a meaning: the yoke off every nation, within two full years. Jeremiah leaves without a further word in that moment.

Arminian readers hear a widened promise and a silence. Jeremiah’s going his way is not yet surrender; it is the pause before the LORD’s word comes, as the next verse will say.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same public saying as Hananiah’s interpretation of the broken bar, and Jeremiah’s departure as the end of this exchange, until the LORD speaks again.

Shared ground: the claim is now for all nations, still within two years. Jeremiah does not settle it on the spot.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, after Hananiah the prophet had broken the bar from off the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, after Hananiah the prophet had broken the bar from off the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying,” The next word is dated after the breaking of the bar. Jeremiah does not invent a reply in the moment; the LORD’s word comes, and he will be sent with it.

Arminian readers take the delay as part of the scene: the word comes from the LORD after the public act, a fresh sending, not a retort Jeremiah had ready in his pocket.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a word that comes from the LORD after the bar is broken, the initiative remaining God’s.

Shared ground: what follows is the LORD’s word, given after Hananiah’s act. The verse is a heading for the message of the next lines.

verses.text: “Go, and tell Hananiah, saying, ‘The LORD says, “You have broken the bars of wood, but you have made in their place bars of iron.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah is sent to tell Hananiah, “You have broken the bars of wood, but you have made in their place bars of iron.” The wooden bars are gone; iron bars stand in their place. The meaning is still plain: a yoke not lighter, but harder, not easily broken as the wood was.

Arminian readers hear a sober reversal of the sign. Hananiah’s act has not freed the nations; it has introduced a heavier service, a word he and the people can still hear in time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sentence as the LORD’s verdict on the broken wood: iron bars in its place, a heavier yoke than the one Hananiah broke.

Shared ground: wood is replaced by iron. The yoke remains the sign of serving Babylon, now described as harder.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and they will serve him. I have also given him the animals of the field.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says, “I have put a yoke of iron on the neck of all these nations, that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and they will serve him. I have also given him the animals of the field.”” The iron yoke is the LORD’s doing, on all these nations, so that they serve the king of Babylon. The gift of the animals of the field recalls 27:6 and should be named without being turned into a new scheme.

Arminian readers hear a confirmed assignment of service, wider than Judah alone, which the nations will in fact render, even after the public breaking of the wooden bar.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the iron yoke as the LORD’s own placing, and the service of Nebuchadnezzar as what will happen, including the gift of the field animals already announced.

Shared ground: the nations will serve, under an iron yoke. The verse answers Hananiah’s “all the nations” with a harder, not a broken, yoke.

verses.text: Then the prophet Jeremiah said to Hananiah the prophet, “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD has not sent you, but you make this people trust in a lie.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Jeremiah said to Hananiah, “Listen, Hananiah! The LORD has not sent you, but you make this people trust in a lie.” After the LORD’s word, Jeremiah speaks plainly. Hananiah is not sent, and the fruit of his speech is that the people trust in a lie. The charge is this lie, in this scene, not a general theory invented for the chapter. Deuteronomy 18:20–22 may again be named by reference as shared ground.

Arminian readers take “The LORD has not sent you” as a verdict now given, and “trust in a lie” as a real harm to the people, who have been led to rely on a word God did not send.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same two clauses as the LORD’s judgment in Jeremiah’s mouth: Hananiah is unsent, and the people have been made to trust in a lie.

Shared ground: the sending is denied, and the people’s trust is called a lie. The traditions need not divide over that verdict.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says, ‘Behold, I will send you away from off the surface of the earth. This year you will die, because you have spoken rebellion against the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore the LORD says, ‘Behold, I will send you away from off the surface of the earth. This year you will die, because you have spoken rebellion against the LORD.’ ” The unsent prophet is himself “sent away” from the earth. The time is this year, and the reason is rebellion spoken against the LORD. The word is as testable as Hananiah’s two years, but far shorter.

Arminian readers hear a dated judgment, spoken so that the hearers can know, within the year, whether this word stands. The cause named is the rebellious speech, not a hidden score.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sentence as the LORD’s: Hananiah will die this year, because he has spoken rebellion against the LORD, and he will be sent away from the surface of the earth.

Shared ground: the death is announced for this year, and the reason is given. The next verse will record what happened.

verses.text: So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.” The announcement is fulfilled in the same year, two months after the fifth-month confrontation, if the heading of verse 1 is followed in a simple count. The notes should not invent a cause of death beyond what the book states, and should not turn the death into a spectacle.

Arminian readers take the short report as the happening of the word Jeremiah had spoken, the very kind of happening 28:9 had named as the way a prophet is known to have been sent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a plain fulfillment: Hananiah dies in the seventh month of the same year, as the LORD had said.

Shared ground: the dated word stands. The verse closes the chapter without a further speech, and without a new contrast to invent.
